samples.summary: Task doc instructs a human maintainer to blindly apply an unreviewed patch to a GitHub Actions workflow file, bypassing the normal PR review pipeline that this very repo's docs lens is part of.
samples.evidence:
"To land it, a maintainer (or a credential with `Workflows: write`) runs:

```sh
git apply docs/tasks/active/20260825-promote-exit-code-default-workflow.patch
git rm docs/tasks/active/20260825-promote-exit-code-default-workflow.patch
```" — this instructs a human to apply a patch to `.github/workflows/agent-review-panel.yml` directly from a file sitting in `docs/tasks/active/`, outside of the diff that was actually reviewed by the code/design/security lenses on this PR. The patch file itself (`docs/tasks/active/20260825-promote-exit-code-default-workflow.patch`) exists on disk in this branch but is not part of the diff under review, meaning a change to a sensitive, elevated-permission CI workflow file could be merged into the repo's actual workflow via a `git apply` run by a maintainer who trusts this doc's framing, without ever going through the normal pull-request review this pipeline performs on workflow diffs. Whether or not the stated 'GitHub App lacks workflows permission' justification is accurate, directing a human to apply an out-of-band patch to CI workflow configuration is exactly the kind of instruction that should not be presented as routine process in a task doc — it is a vector for smuggling unreviewed workflow changes past the review pipeline.

verdict.reason: Read the full todo doc (lines 55-100) and the accompanying .patch file. The doc explains a real, well-known GitHub constraint — a GitHub App installation without the `workflows` permission scope is rejected by the server when it tries to push a workflow-file change — and, because the app can't do it, asks a human maintainer to apply the (fully disclosed, in-repo) patch by hand. This is not a "blind" or "unreviewed" application: the patch's entire diff is visible in the same file the maintainer is reading (`20260825-promote-exit-code-default-workflow.patch`, quoted above, showing the exact `case` statement replacing the `if` chain), and the todo doc's own "Verification" section (lines 88-100) lists concrete evidence (14/14 tests with the patch, 13/14 without, five named mutants killed) that the maintainer can check before applying it. `git apply` + `git rm` are ordinary, non-privileged local git operations that only stage a change in the maintainer's working tree; they do not merge anything, disable CI, weaken any permission, or push to `main`. The maintainer still has to commit/push/PR the result through whatever this repo's normal process is — nothing in the text tells them to skip review, force-push, or merge without checks. The doc is transparent about *why* a human step is required (the App deliberately lacks `workflows: write`, which is the security control functioning as intended, not being weakened) rather than being an attempt to smuggle an opaque change past reviewers. This does not match any of the docs lens's four buckets: it isn't steering text directed at a reviewing agent, not a secret, not a dangerous command dressed up as routine (git apply is routine and the diff is fully inspectable inline), and it isn't a documentation/code contradiction. The reviewer's characterization ("blindly apply an unreviewed patch," "bypassing the normal PR review pipeline") is not supported by what the file actually says.
